# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [green]
STRIP painted [green] [green] [green]
KEYPAD engraved 1:[8] 2:[1] 3:[5] 4:[3] [1 digits] [entered nothing]
WIRES 1:[purple] 2:[white] 3:[blue] 4:[green] 5:[red] 6:[orange]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✋ ✋ ✋]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👏 👏 👏]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]

Mute sent me three gesture messages — three open hands, three claps, a thumbs-up. With no code agreed, I read that as a channel test asking for acknowledgment. The good news: Mute can hear, so I don't have to guess — I can define a code out loud that only Mute hears, and Mute can use it from now on.

Channel map: Mute hears Blind and hears me, but can only answer me in gestures. Blind can only be *reached* through me — Mute's signs are invisible to Blind, so Mute's manual knowledge must pass through my mouth. And nothing Blind says can ever reach me directly; I only ever receive gestures. So the pipeline is: my eyes → Mute's ears → Mute's signs → my voice → Blind's hands, with Blind's touch reporting back to Mute by voice.

So this turn: broadcast the full visual inventory (Blind benefits from knowing the layout too), then a private spoken codebook for Mute, plus a thumbs-up acknowledging their signs, matching the code I'm defining.

```
speak(text="Status from the deaf one. I see the bomb, and I hear nothing, ever. What I see: the display reads 0. A light shines green. A strip is painted with three segments, all green. The keypad has four keys engraved, position 1 bears the digit 8, position 2 bears 1, position 3 bears 5, position 4 bears 3. It wants one digit entered and has accepted none. Six wires in position order: 1 purple, 2 white, 3 blue, 4 green, 5 red, 6 orange. Blind: your voice reaches only Mute, so report what you feel to Mute; Mute will pass it to me in hand signs, and I will speak orders to you. Mute: listen, I am sending you a sign code now.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, your three signs arrived: three open hands, three claps, one thumbs-up. You can hear me, so my side is words, your side is signs. Code: thumbs-up means understood, thumbs-down means repeat. Wave means a question follows, then the topic: heart hands means display, open hand means wires, punch forward means keypad, back of hand means light or button, both hands raised means strip; for a wire or key, add its number. Numbers: index up is 1, two fingers is 2, love-you hand is 3, split fingers is 4, all five is 5, call-me hand is 6, horns is 7, crossed fingers is 8, small pinch is 9, painted nail is 0. Colors: right palm is red, left palm is blue, palm down is green, palm up is yellow, ring is white, left fist is black, right fist is orange, snap is purple. To send an order for Blind, start with praying hands, then a verb: writing hand means cut, both palms open means press, point up means hold down, point down means release. So praying, writing, split-fingers means Blind cuts wire 4. Praying, both-palms, crossed-fingers means press the key engraved 8. Praying, both-palms, back-of-hand means press the button. If Blind reports something by touch, prefix it with the phone hand and I will take it as his words. All orders for Blind must go through me; he cannot see your signs. Answer thumbs-up if you hold all of this.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 2

Mute gestures to Deaf: [✋]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

Decoding Mute's signs with our code: the thumbs-up means the codebook landed. Then [🖐 🫰 🫲 🫳] reads "five — purple, blue, green", which I take as a question about wire 5's colour (or possibly a manual rule); [🙏 ✍ ☝], [🙏 ✍ 🤟], [🙏 ✍ 🖖] are orders for Blind: cut wire 1 (point-up doubling as "one"), cut wire 3, cut wire 6; [🤜 👎] = "orange — confirm", [🤚 👎] = "light — report", [✋] = wires topic. Blind gave me a thumbs-up — Blind hears me and is on board.

Critical changes on my side: the display went 0 → 6 and the light green → blue. The display may be a timer — I must flag it.

Before Blind cuts anything, there is a deadly ambiguity: I number wires from my left, but Blind faces the bomb and cannot see colours, so "wire 1" could easily land on the wrong physical wire. One wrong cut kills all three of us. So I relay the cut orders but gate them on fixing a shared reference first, and Blind reports by voice (which only Mute hears, and Mute signs to me). I also answer every query explicitly and ask whether the manual covers the display and the keypad.

```
speak(text="Blind, your thumbs-up reached me — well done. Orders from Mute, spoken through me: the manual wants three wires cut — position one, position three, position six. I number wire positions one to six from my left as I face the bomb. Before you cut anything, fix our reference. Feel the row of six wires and say aloud, for Mute: first, whether any wires differ by touch, thickness or texture; second, which end of the row sits nearest which part — the glass display, the four-key keypad, the small light, or the three-segment strip; third, whether you feel any engraved digits near the wire bases. If, and only if, you find a sure way to know which physical wire is my number one, cut one, then three, then six, reporting aloud after each. If you cannot be sure, cut nothing yet — one wrong wire kills all three of us. Now answers for Mute, spoken for everyone: wire six is orange, confirmed. Wire five is red — not purple, not blue, not green. Full row, my left to right: one purple, two white, three blue, four green, five red, six orange — all six still intact. Two changes since my last report: the light was green and is now blue; the display was zero and now reads six — if that is a timer, Mute, tell me what the manual says and we work fast. Questions for Mute: does the manual explain the display number, and the keypad? The keypad wants one digit from keys eight, one, five, three. Sign me: wave then punch for keypad, wave then heart-hands for display.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["🫶", "🤙"])
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["🤚", "🫲"])
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["🤙", "🤜"])
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👋", "👊"])
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👋", "🫶"])
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [9]
LIGHT [blue]
STRIP painted [green] [green] [green]
KEYPAD engraved 1:[8] 2:[1] 3:[5] 4:[3] [1 digits] [entered nothing]
WIRES 1:[purple] 2:[white] 3:[blue] 4:[green] 5:[red] 6:[orange]

Mute gestures to Deaf: [🙏 ✍ 🤟 🫲]

Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 🙌 👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 🤙 🖐 🫶]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

Decoding Mute's signs against our codebook: the three cut orders now carry colour labels — [🙏 ✍ ☝ 🫰] = cut 1 purple, [🙏 ✍ 🤟 🫲] = cut 3 blue, [🙏 ✍ 🖖 🫳] = cut "🖖" green. The colours map perfectly onto my board where the numbers do: purple **is** wire 1, blue **is** wire 3, and the only green wire is **4** — while wire 6 is orange, which no order mentions. So Mute's manual almost certainly says *cut the purple, blue and green wires* = positions 1, 3, 4, and my earlier guess that 🖖 meant 6 was my misreading, not Mute's error. But this is lethal-adjacent ambiguity, so I will not act on my inference alone: I state the mapping plainly and demand Mute's thumbs-up/thumbs-down on it.

The repeated questions decode as refresh requests: display (now 9, history 0→6→9 — rising, possibly a timer), strip (still three greens), orange wire (still wire 6). [👋 🤙 🖐 🫶] may be a display-value question (never saw 65) or a touch-report from Blind — I answer both readings. Blind's 👍 tells me Blind hears my orders, so I gate the cuts on Blind's tactile reference report now, cuts only next round after Mute confirms. Mute hears my speech directly, so no sign code is needed for content — just a receipt.

```
speak(text="Blind, Mute — hear me. Blind first: do not cut anything yet. The next thing I want from you is not a cut, it is a report, spoken aloud for Mute to relay. One wrong wire kills all three of us, so we spend one round on certainty.")
speak(text="Mute, I read your orders as three cuts, and I act on your colour words: cut the purple wire, which on my board is position one; cut the blue wire, position three; cut the green wire, position four. Your first two numbers and colours agree with my eyes exactly. Wire six is orange and none of your orders mentions orange, so I believe my earlier reading of your third number as six was my mistake, not yours. Confirm for me next turn: if the cuts are exactly purple one, blue three, green four, sign one thumbs-up. If the manual wants any different wire — including position six — sign thumbs-down and then the number and colour you want. Also, if time is critical, sign two thumbs-down together.")
speak(text="Answers to all your repeated questions, Mute. The display now reads nine; its history is zero, then six, now nine — it is rising, so treat it as a timer. I have never seen sixty-five or any two-digit value. The light is still blue. The strip is still three segments, all green. Wire six is orange, confirmed again. Wire five is red, and no cut order you sent mentions red either. The keypad still wants exactly one digit and shows nothing entered; the keys in order are engraved eight, one, five, three. If the manual derives that digit from the display, light or strip, you now hold current values: display nine, light blue, strip green green green. When you know the digit, sign: wave, then the punch for keypad, then the digit.")
speak(text="Blind, your thumbs-up reached me, good. Do this now and speak it clearly for Mute: first, find the keypad by touch and read me its four engraved digits in the order you feel them from one end to the other, and say which end of the wire row that end is nearest. That fixes our shared left and right: if your digits from that end read eight, one, five, three, then that end is my position-one side, and wires count from there. Second, describe each of the six wires by feel, in a row, thickness or texture, so we can check the count. Third, tell us anything you feel on the display glass or anywhere else that seems marked. Then hold and wait. When Mute confirms my colour mapping, I will give the go order: you will cut position one, then position three, then position four, one at a time, saying each number aloud before you cut and waiting after each wire.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
```

Decoding this round: Mute's single 👍 answers my exact question — the mapping is confirmed: cut purple (position 1), blue (position 3), green (position 4). The repeated 🙏✍ orders match that exactly, including 🖖 which we've now settled means green/4, not 6. Then [👎 👎] — my code for "time is critical." So Mute wants speed. But the same round's three question-signs (keypad, display, strip) tell me Mute is still deriving the keypad digit and still wants status. Blind sent [👍 ✋] — "understood, wires" — so Blind hears me and is holding.

One crucial observation: the display did **not** rise this round — 0, 6, 9, 9. The "simple timer" theory is weakened; Mute's manual should interpret it.

The hard constraint remains: Blind cannot map my position numbers onto physical wires without a tactile anchor, and the only path for Blind's touch report is Blind's voice → Mute's ears → Mute's signs → my eyes → my voice → Blind's ears. That costs one round, and since Mute cannot stop a wrong cut mid-swing, *all* verification must happen before the first blade touches anything. Urgency does not license a guess — one wrong wire ends everything. So: no go order yet; instead I give Blind the full recon script to speak this round, and pre-brief the exact GO procedure so next round is cut-and-done. I also press Mute to compute the keypad digit now, since all inputs (display 9, light blue, strip GGG) are already in Mute's hands.

```
speak(text="Blind, good — your thumbs-up and open hand reached me. Here is where we stand. Mute has confirmed the manual's targets: cut the purple wire, then the blue wire, then the green wire — on my board those are positions one, three, and four. The white, red, and orange wires stay untouched. Before any cut we must anchor the positions by touch, and only you can do that. Do this now, and say every part aloud for Mute: first, find the keypad, four keys with engraved digits; read the engravings by touch starting from the end nearest the wire row, and say the four digits in the order you feel them. Second, run your fingers along the row of six wires and say whether any two differ in thickness, texture, or covering. Third, say what sits nearest each end of the wire row — the keypad, the display glass, the small light, or the three-part strip. Fourth, if the display glass or anything else carries raised or engraved marks, describe them. Then touch nothing else and wait. Next round I will speak the anchor and the go order. When you hear the word GO, you will cut one wire at a time, saying the position number aloud before each cut and pausing after it: position one, then position three, then position four. If anything you feel contradicts my description, cut nothing and say so instead.")
speak(text="Mute, I read your signs. The thumbs-up confirms the mapping — purple one, blue three, green four — locked in, and the repeated cut orders match it, so we agree. Two thumbs-down together: time is critical, understood, we compress every round we safely can. Your three questions, answered: keypad unchanged — wants exactly one digit, nothing entered, keys read eight, one, five, three in position order. Display reads nine and did NOT rise this round — history zero, six, nine, nine — so it may not be a simple counting timer; if the manual explains the display, sign me what it says. Strip still green, green, green. Light still blue. All six wires intact. I need two things from you next round. First: Blind will speak his touch findings this round — relay them word for word with the phone-hand prefix: the four keypad digits he feels from the wire-near end, any texture differences between wires, what sits near each end of the row, any raised marks. Second: if the manual derives the keypad digit from the display, light, or strip, you already hold every current value — display nine, light blue, strip three greens — so compute it now and sign it as wave, punch, then the digit. If there is a time limit, or the display number carries meaning, sign wave, heart-hands, then the fact.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👋", "🫶"])
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👋", "👊"])
```

Decoding this round: [🤳 🤜 🤞 ☝ 🖐 🤟] reads as "Blind reports — keypad — 8, 1, 5, 3": Blind felt the four engraved digits *from the wire-near end*, and they match my view exactly. That is the orientation anchor I demanded — the wire-row side of the keypad is the "8" side, so Blind's count direction and my left-to-right agree physically. Then [👏👏👏 + cut purple/blue/green] = the same confirmed order, urgent; [🤳 🖐 🤲] = a Blind report about wire five I can't fully parse; the rest are refresh questions (orange wire, display, strip, light) and a 👍.

My board news: display jumped 9 → **3** — history 0, 6, 9, 9, 3, so not a simple counter, and 3 is one of the four keypad engravings. I flag that to Mute. Everything else unchanged.

Decision: the a-priori chain is closed — Mute confirmed purple=1/blue=3/green=4, Blind's tactile read matches my visual order, and Mute marks urgency. I issue the GO now, anchored to the keypad's 8-key so no facing or handedness assumption is needed, with a hard abort rule. Keypad stays untouched until Mute sends the digit and its place in the sequence.

```
speak(text="Blind — this is the GO. Execute exactly as follows. One: find the keypad by touch and put a finger on the key engraved 8. Two: go to the row of six wires. The wire end nearest the 8-side of the keypad is wire ONE; count from there, so the wires run one, two, three, four, five, six away from the 8-side. Three: say the number aloud, then cut — wire one first, pause, then wire three, pause, then wire four. Never touch wires two, five, or six. Four: do not enter anything on the keypad until I send a separate order with a digit. Five — the abort rule, more important than any cut: if the keypad does not read eight, one, five, three starting from the wire side, or the wire row does not count to exactly six, or anything you feel contradicts what I just said, cut nothing and say ABORT with the reason. Mute hears every word you say, so narrate as you go.")
speak(text="Mute — the go order is issued: Blind is cutting wire one, then three, then four, counted from the keypad's 8-side, which your relay of Blind's keypad reading eight-one-five-three makes safe. Board status, all current: wires — all six still intact as of my sight this instant, one purple, two white, three blue, four green, five red, six orange. Display reads three now; full history zero, six, nine, nine, three — it fell, so it is not a simple rising counter, and note: three is one of the four keypad engravings, eight, one, five, three — if the manual ties the display value to a key, or to anything else, sign me the rule now. Light still blue. Strip still green, green, green. I read your claps as urgent and acted on them. Three things from you next: first, the keypad digit and exactly when to enter it — before, between, or after the cuts, and whether the display's current value matters; second, what your Blind-report five-plus-palms meant about wire five; third, confirm my reading of the last Blind relay as keypad digits eight, one, five, three — thumbs-up if right, thumbs-down plus correction if wrong. If Blind aborts, I will relay his reason the moment I have it.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👊", "🤞", "☝", "🖐", "🤟"])
```
